title: Are You Working: In Defense of the Invisible Labors of Creativitiy
content:
Once, at the gym with a physicist friend, I was struck by how no one else in the room had any idea that while she was sweating on the treadmill with a blank stare into space, she was doing advanced mathematics working out the logic of black holes.

Another time, on the train with a poet friend, none of the other passengers could have known that behind her faraway look she was doing the invisible labor that would eventually win her the Pulitzer.

“Artists are always working, though they may not seem as if they are,” the visionary theater director André Gregory wrote to the visionary photographer Richard Avedon in his courageous antidote to the Cartesian myth of work/life balance. “They are like plants growing in winter. You can’t see the fruit, but it is taking root below the earth.”

We call the titans of creativity “visionaries” precisely because their work is a kind of subterranean vision that only the inner eye can see, indiscernible to any surface observer until it takes a tangible shape — be it a poem or a theorem — that touches the world, that changes it.

Leo Lionni (May 5, 1910–October 11, 1999) offers a timeless defense of this invisible, vital work in Frederick (public library) — his 1968 philosophical postulate disguised as a children’s book.

A wartime refugee from Holland, Lionni went on to become one of America’s most beloved writers and illustrators of children’s books — more than forty of them in his long life (along with innumerable drawings, paintings, and sculptures of wood, metal, and glass), taking on the largest questions of what it means to be alive with extraordinary subtlety masked as simplicity.

A decade after Little Blue and Little Yellow — which he wrote for his own grandkids — offered a foundational understanding of color that went on to influence generations of graphic designers and artists, Frederick offered a foundational understanding of creativity — the mightiest defense of the imagination since William Blake’s famous letter.

Well before philosopher Bernard Suits subverted Aesop’s famous fable to make the grasshopper its hero, not its fool, by demonstrating that play is more rewarding than productivity, Lionni’s kindred story insists that creativity — the key to which Einstein termed “combinatory play” — nourishes more deeply than consumption.

We meet a family of field mice living in a stone wall, working day and night to gather food in preparation for winter — all but one. As the rest toil, Frederick stands still and quiet, staring into space.

“Frederick, why don’t you work?” they ask.

“I do work,” he answers.

He is, rather, laboring — I am thinking of Lewis Hyde’s timeless distinction between work and labor. Frederick is laboring at a lighthouse for dark times: It is not food he is gathering but light and color, images and ideas — those immaterial mercies that make life at its coldest and harshest more livable.

When winter does come, the mice huddle between the stones and begin feasting on their cache, chatting happily about inconsequential things. But little by little, the food runs out, the conversation hollows, and they begin wondering about Frederick’s gatherings.

He instructs them to close their eyes, and suddenly there is magic — his words conjure up light and color in their marveled minds, sealed with a verse he speaks from atop a stone, doing what all artists ultimately do — open the door to the mystery of what it means to be alive:

Who scatters snowflakes? Who melts the ice?
Who spoils the weather? Who makes it nice?
Who grows the four-leaf clovers in June?
Who dims the daylight? Who lights the moon?

Stephen Hawking was asking the same with his eternal question: “What is it that breathes fire into the equations and makes a universe for them to describe?” Frederick’s answer reminds us that we may never know what created us, but that creative force is in us, of us — the divine within:

Four little field mice who live in the sky,
Four little field mice… like you and I.

When Frederick finishes his verse, the other field mice suddenly realize that he is a poet, that he had been doing the poet’s work all along — all through those still silent hours when he appeared to be doing nothing, he was wresting meaning from the bewilderment of being alive, finding the words to praise the brief miracle of it.

Pulsating beneath the story is a reminder that whether the poem is made of words or of mathematics, it is only ever made in the mind — that strange and solitary place where ideas are born like new stars out of the fertile cosmic darkness, molecules of thought pulled together by the gravity of feeling to become light.
